input: …it can be seen that the wall thickness of the compressor casing amounts to 43 mm once the corrosion allowance has been added on top of the thickness required for pressure containment purposes. It is worth emphasising that this additional material is provided to accommodate corrosion over the casing lifetime, rather than being required by the design pressure. With regard to the selection of the gasket material, a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate materials, focusing on the temperature limit. On this basis, the higher-rated material is preferred for the joint in question, since the temperature at the flange face is the condition the gasket must withstand, and it is on this condition that the two materials are most clearly distinguished, whereas their other recorded properties are broadly comparable. The discharge conditions that give rise to this temperature arise from the absorber overhead circuit, whilst the lean solvent pump determines the pressure at which the suction side of the machine operates, meaning that the $\Delta P$ against which the casing has been checked already takes account of both ends of the machine. target: …the compressor casing wall comes to 43 mm once the corrosion allowance is added to the pressure thickness, and the added material is there for the life of the casing rather than for the design pressure alone. The pressure thickness itself is not in dispute; the dispute in the sizing was over how much allowance the corrosion the service produces justifies, and the figure adopted settles that question on the conservative side. On the gaskets, the comparison between the two materials runs on temperature limit only. The higher-rated material takes the joint: the temperature at the flange face is the condition the gasket has to survive, and on that condition the two materials separate cleanly, while on the other properties recorded for them they do not.
